children: U.S. Treasury yields eased Friday after a sharp sell-off earlier in the week but remained elevated as resilient economic growth, persistent inflation, and heavy Treasury issuance continued to put upward pressure on borrowing costs, according to Pantheon Macroeconomics.

The 10-year yield was around 100 bp above its level at the start of the year and roughly 50 bp higher over the past month, Pantheon said. The firm said some repricing was warranted but argued that the latest leg of the Treasury sell-off had gone too far.

fell 3.4 bp to 4.90%, while the 5-year yield (
slipped 2.7 bp to 5.18%, and the 30-year yield

Wednesday's move had been much sharper, with both the 2-year and 10-year yields rising around 15 bp and the 30-year yield climbing about 10 bp. Pantheon said the increase was partly linked to higher energy prices following the Iran war and less encouraging trends in core inflation, while large federal deficits and heavy Treasury issuance had also left the market more fragile than usual.

A stronger-than-expected September S&P Global composite PMI also helped trigger the latest move higher. The index rose to 58.4 from 56.0 in August, its highest level since July 2021, and Pantheon said yields continued to climb for several hours after the release as investors appeared to embrace the stronger-growth story.

Pantheon, however, questioned whether the PMI was a reliable signal of a sustained acceleration in growth, noting that seven of the 10 regional Fed surveys available for September had been much less upbeat. The firm said a sharp and sustained acceleration in GDP growth was unlikely and expected at least some recent rise in Treasury yields to reverse in the near term.
Pantheon projected the 10-year yield at 4.75% by year-end, down from 5.15% in its report, and at 4% by the end of 2027.

title: Latest Treasury sell-off looks overdone, Pantheon says
